prompt.context: Your client is an energy firm that has a lot of extra cash and wants to know if they should consolidate HVAC (heating, ventilation and cooling) service firms in the Atlanta area.
prompt.question: The client would like to know if this is a viable investment they should consider.

clarifying_info.q: How many HVAC firms are in the Atlanta market?
What is the average annual revenue of a target firm?
What is the revenue growth rate?
How is the acquisition cost determined?
What is the cost of capital?
What is the cost structure of these firms?
clarifying_info.a: Labor 50% of revenues, Equipment 25%, Administrative 20%, Profit the remaining 5%

clarifying_info.q: What savings can the client achieve post-acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: Labor dispatching efficiency: 5% decrease in labor costs; Equipment: 5% decrease through bargaining power; Admin: 1% net decrease after IT and advertising investments

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's hurdle for this investment?

clarifying_info.a: Assume all cost savings occur immediately
Assume revenues will remain stable for each target

framework: Determine the acquisition cost per firm using the perpetuity valuation (current profit / (CoC - growth rate))
Model the post-acquisition cost structure: apply savings to each cost line and calculate new profit
Perform a break-even analysis: acquisition cost / new annual profit, and compare to the 3-year threshold
Suggest levers to improve break-even if the base case fails

questions.prompt: Calculate the acquisition cost for a single HVAC firm.
questions.guidance: Use perpetuity formula: Price = Profit / (CoC - growth). Current profit = 5% of $10M = $500K. Interest rate = 13% - 3% = 10%. Cost of firm = $500K / 10% = $5M.

math.setup: Perpetuity price = Annual profit / (Cost of capital - Growth rate)

questions.prompt: Calculate the new annual profit after applying all post-acquisition cost savings.
questions.guidance: Apply each savings percentage to the respective cost base, then compute new total costs and new profit.

math.setup: New profit = Revenue - (new Labor cost + new Equipment cost + new Admin cost)

questions.prompt: Perform an undiscounted break-even analysis and compare it to the 3-year requirement.
questions.guidance: Break-even = Acquisition cost / New annual profit. Result exceeds 3 years, so the investment does NOT meet the hurdle rate.

math.setup: Undiscounted break-even = Acquisition cost / New annual profit
math.answer: ≈5.58 years — TOO LONG, does not meet the 3-year requirement. RECOMMENDATION: NO GO on current terms.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key risks of this consolidation strategy, and what levers could improve the break-even?

categories.name: Risks
ideas: No prior industry experience — the energy firm has no HVAC operational expertise
Cultural issues — small owner-operated firms being absorbed by a large corporation may face employee/management resistance
National entrants — large national HVAC players could enter the Atlanta market and overpower the consolidation effort
Technician retention risk given 100% current utilization

categories.name: Levers to improve break-even
ideas: Reduce purchase price negotiated below perpetuity value
Seek further cost improvements beyond those identified (IT systems, warranty cost pooling, etc.)
Improve revenues through advertising efficiency, brand name development, referrals, and cross-selling
Achieve additional equipment savings via national purchasing agreements
Stagger acquisitions to reduce upfront capital requirement

recommendation: Do NOT proceed with the acquisition on current terms
The undiscounted break-even of ~5.58 years fails the client's 3-year hurdle
The base case new profit of $895K per firm is insufficient to recover the $5M acquisition cost within 3 years
risks: No HVAC industry experience creates operational risk
Cultural friction from absorbing 500 small firms
Competitive risk from national HVAC entrants in Atlanta
next_steps: Negotiate a lower acquisition price per firm to reduce payback period
Identify additional cost savings levers (IT, warranties, procurement)
Model revenue upside from brand consolidation and advertising efficiency
Pilot with a small number of acquisitions before committing to full market roll-up
